```{r opts, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

PlotTrellis draws multi-track genomic figures (coverage, splice junctions, Hi-C, transcript
structures and expression, comparisons between samples) in a point-and-click app or in a few
lines of R.

# Installation

PlotTrellis needs R 4.5 or later. From scratch, installing takes 40 to 50 minutes on Linux
(add `Ncpus = 4` to the second `install.packages()` to speed it up):

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("BiocManager")
install.packages("PlotTrellis", repos = c("https://aleks-wehi.r-universe.dev",
                                          BiocManager::repositories()))
```

# Your first figure in the app

```{r app-example, eval=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("org.Mm.eg.db", quietly = TRUE)) BiocManager::install("org.Mm.eg.db", update = FALSE)   # mouse gene annotation (for human data: "org.Hs.eg.db")
library(PlotTrellis)
run_plottrellis(project_dir = "PlotTrellis-example", samples_txt = pt_example())
```

This opens the bundled example: mouse mammary basal cells (Basal) and luminal progenitors (LP)
around the *Elf5*, *Ehf* and *Cat* genes. `pt_example()` is the path of its `samples.txt`, the
file that lists a project's samples and data. `project_dir` is the folder PlotTrellis keeps the
project in (any folder; without it, `~/PlotTrellis`).

The app opens empty. Click the gene box and pick *Elf5* (it is suggested), pick the samples, add
tracks, then click **Generate figure**. Then try *Ehf* or *Cat*, or other tracks. R is busy while
the app runs: close the app's browser tab to stop it.

A second example, human GM12878 and K562 cells around *PSME2*, has splice junctions too: use
`samples_txt = pt_example("human")` and a new `project_dir` (it needs `org.Hs.eg.db`).

To make your own figure, type a gene (or switch to **Region** for coordinates), then pick the
samples:

```{r compose-screenshot-1, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/sample_and_gene_selection.png")
```

Click tracks under **Add** to put them in the figure (drag to reorder) and click **Generate
figure**. Every figure you generate stays in the strip under it, to go back to or to compare.
**Figure settings** has the title, fonts, heights and colours. **SVG** and **R script** download
the figure and a script that redraws it, and **Gene info** shows the gene's transcripts and
protein domains. Press **?** for the keyboard shortcuts.

```{r compose-screenshot-2, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/track_composer.png")
```

Working in R instead? See [Your first figure in code](#your-first-figure-in-code).

# Your own data

Run the command with a new `project_dir` and no `samples_txt`:

```{r own-data, eval=FALSE}
run_plottrellis(project_dir = "my-project")
```

A wizard asks for your genome, data folder and samples, and saves them in the project folder
as `project_samples.txt`. Click **Save and open the app**: the app reopens in a new tab (if
not, its address is in the R console). To come back, run the same command. To quit the wizard
without saving, stop R's command (Esc in RStudio, Ctrl+C in a terminal).

```{r wizard-screenshot, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/wizard_manual.png")
```

# Your genome: GTF, OrgDb and genome label

Every project needs three things about its genome, asked for by the wizard or given in a
`samples.txt` header. PlotTrellis works with mouse and human.

- **The GTF** (`gtf_path`): the gene annotation file, gzipped or not. Use GENCODE or Ensembl,
  not RefSeq, from the same release your Salmon index was built from: a transcript the GTF
  lacks is left out of the expression tracks. For GENCODE, Salmon must have been run with
  `--gencode`. The first use of a GTF takes 1 to 3 minutes.
- **The OrgDb package** (`orgdb`): `org.Mm.eg.db` or `org.Hs.eg.db`, installed once with
  `BiocManager::install()`. It finds genes by name. A gene it has no name for (some lncRNAs
  and `Gm` genes) can still be shown by its coordinates.
- **The genome label** (`genome_label`): the build's UCSC name. Its first use needs internet.

| Species, build | GENCODE releases | Ensembl releases | `orgdb` | `genome_label` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mouse, GRCm39 | M26 and later | 103 and later | `org.Mm.eg.db` | `mm39` |
| Mouse, GRCm38 | M25 and earlier | 68 to 102 | `org.Mm.eg.db` | `mm10` |
| Human, GRCh38 | 20 and later | 76 and later | `org.Hs.eg.db` | `hg38` |
| Human, GRCh37 | 3c to 19 (not the "lift37" files) | 55 to 75, or the GRCh37 archive | `org.Hs.eg.db` | `hg19` |

The build must be the one your reads were aligned to. GENCODE gives the most: Ensembl GTFs
lack APPRIS labels, and releases before GENCODE 38 (mouse M27) or Ensembl 104 mark no
transcript as Ensembl canonical.

Type regions with `chr` (`chr2:103300000-103500000`), even with an Ensembl GTF. Your data
files can name chromosomes either way (`chr2` or `2`).

Downloads:

- GENCODE: [human](https://www.gencodegenes.org/human/) or
  [mouse](https://www.gencodegenes.org/mouse/), the "Comprehensive gene annotation" GTF
  (region "CHR"). Older releases are under "Releases".
- Ensembl: `https://ftp.ensembl.org/pub/release-<N>/gtf/<species>/`, the file
  `<Species>.<build>.<N>.gtf.gz`, e.g.
  [Mus_musculus.GRCm38.100.gtf.gz](https://ftp.ensembl.org/pub/release-100/gtf/mus_musculus/).
  Human GRCh37 is under `https://ftp.ensembl.org/pub/grch37/`.

# Your first figure in code

The example figure from the app:

```{r code-example, eval=FALSE}
library(PlotTrellis)
proj <- pt_project(project_dir = "PlotTrellis-example", samples_txt = pt_example())
fig  <- pt_figure(proj, "Elf5", tracks = c("atac", "transcript_expression", "transcripts_annotated", "genes"))
pt_save(fig, "Elf5.pdf")   # or .svg, .png
```

```{r code-example-run, echo=FALSE, fig.alt="Elf5 in mouse mammary basal cells and luminal progenitors: ATAC coverage and transcript expression for each, then the annotated transcripts and the gene."}
library(PlotTrellis)
proj <- pt_project(project_dir = file.path(tempdir(), "PlotTrellis-example"), samples_txt = pt_example())
pt_figure(proj, "Elf5", tracks = c("atac", "transcript_expression", "transcripts_annotated", "genes"))
```

# Your own data in code (writing a samples.txt)

A `samples.txt` is a tab-separated table, one row per sample, under a few `#` header lines.
This example has real tabs, so copying it works:

```
# data_root: /data/smithlab/tcell_2026
# gtf_path: /data/reference/gencode.v44.annotation.gtf.gz
# orgdb: org.Hs.eg.db
# genome_label: hg38
condition	colour	bw:atac	paired-end:junctions	quantdir:salmon
Control	#1b9e77	atac/Control_merged.bw	junctions/Control_SJ.bed	salmon/Control
KO	#d95f02	atac/KO_merged.bw	junctions/KO_SJ.bed	salmon/KO
```

The header lines:

- `data_root`: the folder your data is in. The table's paths are relative to it.
- `gtf_path`, `orgdb`, `genome_label`: your genome (see above).
- Optional: any app setting, e.g. `# fontsize: 12` (a project's `project_samples.txt` lists the
  ones changed in the app).

The columns:

- `condition`: the sample's name.
- `colour` (optional): the sample's colour.
- One column per data type, headed `type:name`: `bw:atac` holds bigWig files and makes tracks
  called `atac`. Leave a cell empty if a sample lacks that data.
- Tracks with the same name share one scale, and comparison tracks (one sample against
  another, e.g. `atac_diff`) need a name both samples have. So use one column per data type, not one per sample. Names are case-sensitive. Wrong:

  ```
  condition	bw:Grans ATAC	bw:pDC ATAC	hic:Grans HiC	hic:pDC HiC
  Grans	atac/Grans.bw		hic/Grans.hic	
  pDC		atac/pDC.bw		hic/pDC.hic
  ```

  Right:

  ```
  condition	bw:ATAC	hic:HiC
  Grans	atac/Grans.bw	hic/Grans.hic
  pDC	atac/pDC.bw	hic/pDC.hic
  ```

| Type | File | Track |
|---|---|---|
| `bw` | bigWig | coverage (ATAC-seq, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq) |
| `quantdir` | a Salmon output folder (with `quant.sf`) | `transcript_expression` |
| `paired-end` | BED12 or BED6 junctions, STAR `SJ.out.tab`, BEDPE, or a HiCCUPS loop file | arcs (splice junctions, loops) |
| `hic` | `.hic`, `.cool`, `.mcool` | Hi-C contact map |
| `bed` | BED, narrowPeak, broadPeak (3 or more columns) | intervals (peaks, regions) |

`bed` and `paired-end` files can be gzipped. An arc's height is its count: the score column
(BED column 5, BEDPE column 8) or an `SJ.out.tab`'s unique reads.

Open it like the example: `run_plottrellis(project_dir = "my-project", samples_txt =
"path/to/samples.txt")`. After you edit your `samples.txt`, the same command updates the
project.

## Let an AI assistant write it

A chat AI (ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot or another) can write your `samples.txt` with you. Paste
the prompt below into a new chat; it asks for a list of your files, checks them and ends with
the file. It also has its own page: `vignette("samples-txt-ai-prompt", package = "PlotTrellis")`.

<details><summary>The prompt (click to open, then Copy)</summary>

```{r ai-prompt, echo=FALSE, comment=""}
cat(readLines(system.file("samples_txt_ai_prompt.md", package = "PlotTrellis", mustWork = TRUE)), sep = "\n")
```

</details>

# More in code

Tracks are listed top to bottom; `pt_tracks(proj)` lists the project's. Annotation tracks such
as `genes` and `transcripts_annotated` need no sample. The rest are drawn for every sample, in
`samples.txt` order, unless you say which. All options: `?pt_figure`.

- **`samples = "LP"`** draws every track for that one sample. A `samples` as long as `tracks`
  gives each track its own, `NA` for tracks that need none:
  `tracks = c("atac", "atac", "genes"), samples = c("LP", "Basal", NA)`.
- **`comparison = c("Basal", "LP")`** draws those two samples, in that order, and gives
  comparison tracks the first as the reference:
  `pt_figure(proj, "Elf5", c("atac", "atac_diff", "genes"), comparison = c("Basal", "LP"))`.
- **`order = "sample"`** groups the tracks by sample instead of by track. Tracks without a
  sample stay where they are written, so put them first or last.
- **Numbers** work instead of names, e.g. `tracks = c(6, 1), samples = 2`, as listed by
  `pt_tracks(proj)` and `pt_samples(proj)`. They change when `samples.txt` does, so use names
  in scripts you keep.
- **`region = "chr2:103,400,000-103,460,000"`** instead of a gene shows any coordinates.
- **Many genes in one file**: put the figures in a list and call
  `pt_stitch(figs, "all_genes.pdf")` (`ncol = 2` for side by side; see `?pt_stitch`).
- **`pt_script(fig, "Elf5.R")`** writes an R script that redraws the figure, for edits the
  API doesn't offer.
- **`run_plottrellis(proj)`** opens the project in the app.

# Sharing

To share a project, send the path to your `samples.txt` (for a wizard project, the
`project_samples.txt` in its folder). The other person runs:

```{r sharing, eval=FALSE}
run_plottrellis(project_dir = "tcell-project",
                samples_txt = "/data/smithlab/tcell_2026/samples.txt")
```

They must be able to read your data files and GTF, so keep them on a shared drive and give
`data_root` and `gtf_path` as full paths. Their project is their own copy. When you edit your
`samples.txt`, their next run picks up the edit and replaces the settings they changed in the
app.

# Troubleshooting

Everything a project keeps (settings, a copy of its samples table, caches) is in its
`project_dir`; your data files stay where they are. The app's **Edit project settings** shows
the folder. Close the app first, then:

- **A figure looks stale**: delete the `cache/` folder inside it (or in the app: Edit project
  settings, Advanced, Clear all caches). The next start rebuilds it in 1 to 3 minutes, which
  needs internet.
- **To start fresh**: delete the `project_dir` and create the project again from your
  `samples.txt`. A wizard project's only samples table is its `project_samples.txt`: copy it
  somewhere else first. Deleting is safe only if the folder holds nothing else, so never use
  your data folder as a `project_dir`.

<style>
.code-box { position: relative; margin: 0 150px 0.5em 0; }
@media screen and (max-width: 991px) { .code-box { margin-right: 0; } }
.code-box pre { margin: 0; }
.copy-code { position: absolute; top: 4px; right: 4px; font-size: 12px; }
</style>
<script>
if (navigator.clipboard) document.querySelectorAll("pre").forEach(function (pre) {
  var button = document.createElement("button");
  button.className = "copy-code";
  button.textContent = "Copy";
  var code = pre.querySelector("code") || pre;
  var box = document.createElement("div");
  box.className = "code-box";
  pre.parentNode.insertBefore(box, pre);
  box.appendChild(pre);
  button.onclick = function () {
    navigator.clipboard.writeText(code.innerText).then(function () {
      button.textContent = "Copied";
      setTimeout(function () { button.textContent = "Copy"; }, 1500);
    });
  };
  box.appendChild(button);
});
</script>
